name: Dark Walnut
lede: Dark Walnut is a near-black brown named for the wood, listed in our data only through a Japanese traditional color source, and one of the most common colors in our painting archive.

sections.title: A wood's name, thinly recorded
sections.body:
Our naming data classes Dark Walnut as a plant-and-landscape word, after the tree and its wood, rather than a pigment [1]. As with [[dark-peacock|Dark Peacock]], it is not recorded in Ridgway's 1912 atlas or the ISCC-NBS lists of 1955; our only traced source is a Japanese traditional color list, undated in that source [1]. The hex, #352925, maps to a computed ISCC-NBS-style classification of "dark grayish brown," about 5.1 units from that block's center, even though no ISCC-NBS entry carries this exact name [1]. In LCH terms it measures lightness 18, chroma 7, hue 45 degrees: very dark and only lightly saturated [1].

Its nearest distinct neighbor by computed color distance is [[pale-black-tone|Pale Black-Tone]], 2.8 units away and read in our data as "almost the same" [2]. One step further is [[zulu|Zulu]], 3.2 units off, also "almost the same" [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a close match covers enough of the canvas in 2,803, as photographed, which puts it above 98 percent of the named colors we track by frequency, among the most common in the whole archive [3]. It peaks in paintings from the 1600s, where it is found at 1.2 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive [3]. Eastman Johnson is its most devoted painter here, with the color present in 6 of 18 of his works, well above the baseline of the museums those works come from [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in 44 percent of its matches, by lightness rank within the canvas [3].
